issues.legal_issue: Royalty collected on extracted minor minerals need not be used exclusively for mineral development.
material_facts: The challenged rules required holders of quarry leases and other mineral concessions to pay royalty on minor minerals removed or consumed from leased areas.
The challengers argued that the royalty became part of the State’s consolidated fund and could not be spent on purposes other than mineral development.
issues.conclusion: The royalty need not be earmarked exclusively for mineral development and may be used for other purposes permitted by law.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, the Court treated royalty on extracted minerals as a tax, not a fee confined to a specific purpose. Tax revenue forms part of the State’s consolidated fund and may be used for purposes within the State’s executive authority, subject to applicable law. Entry 50 of List II does not require that the revenue be spent only on mineral development.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rule_challenge: The case challenges a royalty imposed under rules governing concessions to extract minor minerals.
predicates.royalty_is_a_tax_on_extracted_minerals: The payment is imposed on minerals extracted under a concession and is treated as a tax rather than a fee for a specific service.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a tax on extracted minor minerals, the rule means that the revenue need not be earmarked exclusively for mineral development.

issues.legal_issue: A royalty imposed under a central law on the right to extract government-owned minerals does not violate the constitutional restriction on State laws restricting trade.
material_facts: The royalty was imposed under rules made pursuant to a central law.
The royalty was payable by persons granted rights to extract minerals belonging to the Government, and the challengers sought to exploit the mines for profit.
issues.conclusion: The levy did not violate the constitutional restriction on State laws imposing restrictions on trade because it was imposed under central law, not State legislation; the Court also found that the royalty did not restrict the challengers’ freedom of trade.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the restriction contemplated by Article 304(b) applies to an imposition made by a State Legislature, whereas this levy was made under central law. It also reasoned that a person seeking an exclusive right to exploit government-owned minerals for profit must pay royalty imposed in accordance with law.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rule_challenge: The case challenges a royalty imposed under rules governing concessions to extract minor minerals.
predicates.levy_is_imposed_under_central_law: The royalty is imposed under rules made pursuant to a law enacted by the central legislature.
predicates.mineral_extraction_requires_a_paid_exclu: A person must pay for the right to exploit government-owned minerals to the exclusion of others and remove them for profit.

issues.definition: When a minor-mineral royalty challenge concerns a levy made under central law for an exclusive extraction right, the rule means that the levy does not violate the restriction on State laws restricting trade.

issues.legal_issue: A challenged royalty rate is not unreasonably high or arbitrary merely because other regions charge less, where the challengers do not establish that the rate is excessive or that their business has been adversely affected.
material_facts: The royalty rate for the minerals had been increased from an earlier rate, and the challengers relied on lower royalty rates in other States to argue that the new rate was excessive.
The Court had previously upheld the earlier rate.

The Court considered the depreciation in the value of money and increases in the cost of State administration, and the challengers had not shown that their business was adversely affected in a way warranting invalidation.
issues.conclusion: The Court found that the challengers had not established that the rate was unreasonably high or arbitrarily imposed.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of establishing that a levy is unreasonably heavy rests on the challenger; lower rates elsewhere do not alone establish excessiveness. As explained in D.K. Trivedi & Sons v. State of Gujarat, the possibility that discretionary power may be abused does not invalidate the power itself, although an actually arbitrary exercise may be set aside. The Court also considered the previously upheld rate, the depreciation in the value of money, and increasing administrative costs.

rule.if: minor_mineral_royalty_rate_challenge and only_lower_rates_elsewhere_are_shown and earlier_rate_was_upheld and public_costs_have_increased and not_adverse_business_effect_is_shown

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rate_challenge: The case challenges the amount of royalty payable for extracting minor minerals.
predicates.only_lower_rates_elsewhere_are_shown: The challengers rely on lower royalty rates in other regions without showing that this comparison establishes that the challenged rate is excessive.
predicates.earlier_rate_was_upheld: A previously applicable rate for the same kind of mineral royalty had been upheld by a court.
predicates.public_costs_have_increased: The value of money has depreciated or the costs of public administration have increased since the earlier rate was set.
predicates.not_adverse_business_effect_is_shown: The challengers do not show that the levy has adversely affected their business in a way that warrants invalidation.

issues.definition: Where a royalty-rate challenge rests only on lower rates elsewhere, an earlier rate had been upheld, public costs have increased, and adverse business effect is not shown, the rule means that the rate is not invalid as unreasonably high or arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: Concessions in royalty obligations for limited-area permit holders and small-scale village potters do not violate equal protection when the classification is reasonable and connected to the purpose of the rules.
material_facts: The rules required quarrying permit holders to pay a reduced royalty and exempted certain village potters from royalty in specified circumstances.
A quarrying permit was limited to a small plot and a short period, and the rules gave priority to individuals who did physical excavation work, including members of disadvantaged communities.
A full quarry lease could cover a larger area and last longer than a quarrying permit.
issues.conclusion: The concessions and exemptions were not discriminatory because they applied to reasonably distinct classes and were connected to the policy of the rules and the social policy of assisting weaker sections.
issues.legal_principle: A classification satisfies Article 14 if it rests on an intelligible differentia separating those included from those excluded and that differentia has a reasonable nexus to the object of the law or rule. The Court held that legislative rule-making power carries, by necessary implication, the power to make equitable classifications to implement the policy of the governing law; no express grant of that specific power is required.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rule_challenge: The case challenges a royalty rule governing concessions to extract minor minerals.
predicates.royalty_concession_applies_to_limited_sc: The rule gives reduced royalty or an exemption to holders of limited-scale permits or to small-scale producers meeting specified conditions.
predicates.permit_rights_are_more_restricted_than_l: The permitted area or duration is substantially more limited than the area or duration available under a full lease.
predicates.concession_targets_weaker_or_small_scale: The concession is directed to people engaged in small-scale or physical extraction work or to other disadvantaged groups.

issues.definition: When a royalty concession benefits limited-scale permit holders whose rights are more restricted than full leases and is directed to weaker or small-scale groups, the rule means that the concession is a valid reasonable classification.

issues.legal_issue: A royalty on quarrying does not violate the constitutional freedom of movement of trade where movement of goods between States is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.
material_facts: The challenged levy applied to quarrying minor minerals.
The Court found that quarrying itself did not involve movement of goods between States and that any later removal of minerals outside the State was not a direct consequence of quarrying.
issues.conclusion: The levy did not violate the constitutional freedom of trade and movement between States.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that quarrying does not itself involve inter-State movement and that any later movement of minerals outside the State is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rule_challenge: The case challenges a royalty imposed on the extraction of minor minerals.
predicates.quarrying_does_not_itself_move_goods_bet: The quarrying activity does not itself involve movement of the extracted goods from one State to another.
predicates.later_outbound_movement_is_not_a_direct_: Any later transport of minerals outside the State is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.

issues.definition: When quarrying does not itself move goods between States and any later outbound movement is not its direct consequence, the rule means that the royalty does not violate inter-State trade and movement freedom.
